```{r}
library(tidyverse)

library(readr)
library(tidymodels)
library(stringr)

team_offense <- read_csv(here("data","weekly_team_stats_offense.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
```

```{r}
normalize_game_id <- function(x){
  x |>
    str_replace_all("_SD_","_LAC_") |>
    str_replace_all("_OAK_","_LVR_") |>
    str_replace_all("_STL_","_LAR_") |>
    str_replace_all("_LA_","_LAR_")
}

normalize_team <- function(x){
  case_when(
    x=="LV"~"LVR",
    x=="LA"~"LAR",
    TRUE~x
  )
}
```

```{r}
games_reg <- games_all |>
  filter(schedule_season>=2012, schedule_playoff==FALSE) |>
  mutate(schedule_week=as.integer(schedule_week)) |>
  left_join(team_lookup, by=c("team_home"="team_name")) |>
  rename(home_team=team) |>
  left_join(team_lookup, by=c("team_away"="team_name")) |>
  rename(away_team=team) |>
  mutate(
    team_favorite_id=normalize_team(team_favorite_id),
    game_id_norm=str_c(
      schedule_season,"_",
      str_pad(schedule_week,2,pad="0"),"_",
      away_team,"_",home_team
    )
  )
```

```{r}
games_team <- games_reg |>
  transmute(
    game_id_norm,
    season=schedule_season,
    week=schedule_week,
    season_type="REG",
    team_norm=home_team,
    opponent=away_team,
    home_away="home",
    team_favorite_id,
    team_score=score_home,
    opponent_score=score_away,
    spread_favorite,
    over_under_line,
    stadium,
    stadium_neutral,
    weather_temperature,
    weather_wind_mph,
    weather_humidity
  ) |>
  bind_rows(
    games_reg |>
      transmute(
        game_id_norm,
        season=schedule_season,
        week=schedule_week,
        season_type="REG",
        team_norm=away_team,
        opponent=home_team,
        home_away="away",
        team_favorite_id,
        team_score=score_away,
        opponent_score=score_home,
        spread_favorite,
        over_under_line,
        stadium,
        stadium_neutral,
        weather_temperature,
        weather_wind_mph,
        weather_humidity
      )
  )
```

```{r}
team_offense_clean <- team_offense |>
  mutate(
    game_id_norm=normalize_game_id(game_id),
    team_norm=normalize_team(team)
  )

team_defense_clean <- team_defense |>
  mutate(
    game_id_norm=normalize_game_id(game_id),
    team_norm=normalize_team(team)
  )
```

```{r}
model_data <- games_team |>
  left_join(
    team_offense_clean,
    by=c("game_id_norm","season","week","season_type","team_norm")
  ) |>
  left_join(
    team_defense_clean,
    by=c("game_id_norm","season","week","season_type","team_norm"),
    suffix=c("_off","_def")
  )
```

```{r}
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    spread_team=if_else(team_norm==team_favorite_id,spread_favorite,-spread_favorite),
    margin=team_score-opponent_score,
    margin_vs_spread=margin+spread_team,
    cover=case_when(
      margin_vs_spread>0~"cover",
      margin_vs_spread<0~"no_cover",
      TRUE~"push"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(cover!="push") |>
  mutate(
    cover=factor(cover),
    home_away=factor(home_away),
    stadium_neutral=factor(stadium_neutral)
  )
```

```{r}
tom_cleaned_model_nfl <- model_data |>
```

## Question

My goal is to predict whether an NFL team covers the closing betting spread. The response variable is spread coverage, which indicates whether a team performed better than the market expectation. I treat this as a binary classification problem with two outcomes: cover and no_cover.

Predicting spread outcomes is difficult because betting markets incorporate large amounts of public and expert information. Because of this, a naive strategy usually performs around 50%. The purpose of this project is to evaluate whether structured statistical models can detect predictive signal beyond the betting market baseline.

## Data Source 


This project combines three NFL datasets. The first dataset contains weekly team offensive statistics. These include yards, pass attempts, rushing attempts, touchdowns, and efficiency metrics. Many variables also include rolling averages that summarize recent team performance. The second dataset contains weekly team defensive statistics. These include sacks, tackles, interceptions, and other defensive performance metrics. The third dataset contains historical NFL betting data. This includes game results, point spreads, totals, stadium information, and weather conditions. All datasets share common identifiers such as season, week, and team. I use these identifiers to join the datasets into a single team-game modeling dataset.

## Data Set Work

My project has a very tough cleaning routine. I needed to consult a lot of online sources to figure out how to fix the various issues. However, I am in a pretty good place. The final modeling dataset is called tom_cleaned_model_nfl. Each row represents a team in a specific game. The response variable is the binary spread coverage outcome.To construct the modeling dataset, I first standardized team identifiers because historical NFL datasets often use different abbreviations across seasons (for example SD vs LAC or OAK vs LVR). I then created a unique game identifier using the season, week, and participating teams so that statistics from different sources could be aligned correctly. Next, I reshaped the game-level betting dataset so that each game appears twice, once from the perspective of the home team and once from the perspective of the away team. This allowed the data to be represented at the team–game level, which is the unit needed for predicting whether a team covers the spread. Finally, I joined the offensive and defensive team statistics to this structure using the shared identifiers, creating a unified dataset that combines betting market information, game context variables, and team performance metrics.


Predictors include betting market variables, game context variables, and team performance statistics. These include variables such as the point spread, weather conditions, offensive production averages, and defensive metrics.

Rows with missing values for the key predictor average_total_off_yards were removed to ensure consistent model input. After cleaning, the dataset contains several thousand observations and more than fifteen predictor variables, which satisfies the project complexity requirements.

## Modeling Plan

I split the dataset into training and testing sets using an 80/20 split, stratified by the response variable. Model performance is estimated using 10-fold cross-validation on the training data.

For Progress Memo 2, I implemented two model - a null baseline model and a logistic regression classifier.

A basic preprocessing recipe is used for both models. The recipe removes zero-variance predictors, converts categorical predictors into dummy variables, and normalizes numeric predictors. This setup creates a simple but complete modeling pipeline that can be expanded later with additional model types and feature engineering. Model performance will primarily be evaluated using ROC AUC because it measures the model’s ability to correctly rank outcomes across different probability thresholds. Accuracy is also reported for interpretability. See my r scripts for this work.





```{r}
data_split <- initial_split(
  tom_cleaned_model_nfl,
  prop = 0.80,
  strata = cover
)

train_data <- training(data_split)

test_data <- testing(data_split)
```


```{r}
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(
  train_data,
  v = 10,
  strata = cover
)
```

```{r}
basic_recipe <- recipe(cover ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```


```{r}
null_mod <- null_model() |>
  set_engine("parsnip") |>
  set_mode("classification")
```

```{r}
null_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_model(null_mod) |>
  add_recipe(basic_recipe)
```

```{r}
null_results <- fit_resamples(
  null_workflow,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)
```



```{r}
log_mod <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")
```

```{r}
log_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_model(log_mod) |>
  add_recipe(basic_recipe)
```

```{r}
log_results <- fit_resamples(
  log_workflow,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)
```



```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-results
#| tbl-cap: "CV performance of the null model and logistic regression model"
#| echo: false


null_metrics <- collect_metrics(null_results) |>
  mutate(model = "Null")

log_metrics <- collect_metrics(log_results) |>
  mutate(model = "Logistic Regression")

model_results <- bind_rows(null_metrics, log_metrics)

model_results |>
  select(model, .metric, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = .metric,
    values_from = mean
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```


## Initial Model Checks

Table @tbl-model-results reports the cross-validated performance of the two initial models (null and logistic regression). The null model produced an accuracy and ROC AUC of 0.50, which represents random guessing. The logistic regression model improved performance, achieving roughly 0.60 accuracy and 0.65 ROC AUC, indicating that the predictors contain real signal. In the context of sports betting, this improvement is meaningful because point spreads are designed so outcomes are close to 50/50, making even small predictive advantages difficult to achieve. In practice, bettors must win roughly 52–53% of bets just to break even, so any model that consistently predicts above 50% suggests a potentially valuable edge and confirms that the modeling pipeline is working.


## Progress and Next Steps

Most of the data cleaning and dataset construction is now complete. The modeling pipeline has been successfully implemented using tidymodels, including data splitting, cross-validation, preprocessing, and baseline model fitting.

For Progress Memo 2 I focused on getting a simple but complete modeling workflow running end-to-end. The null model and logistic regression model both fit successfully and produced reasonable results.

The next steps of the project will focus on expanding the modeling framework. I plan to implement several additional model types including random forest, gradient boosted trees, k-nearest neighbors, and elastic net logistic regression. I will also experiment with additional feature engineering and alternative recipes to improve predictive performance.
